question: v02
q: How bad is the rent situation in Sydney?

transcript.answer:
Sydney rents are still rising, but much more slowly than at the 2023–24 peak. They are now growing a little slower than overall prices.

**Annual rent inflation in Sydney (ABS CPI, rents component)**

| Period | Sydney | Australia |
|---|---|---|
| Aug 2023 | 8.7% | 7.8% |
| Mar 2024 (peak) | 8.8% | 7.7% |
| Aug 2024 | 7.1% | 6.7% |
| Aug 2025 | 3.2% | 3.7% |
| Aug 2026 (latest) | 3.5% | 3.6% |

- **Peak:** Sydney rent growth peaked at 8.8% a year in March 2024, and was above 8% from mid-2023 to early 2024.
- **Easing:** It fell to a low of 3.2% in Aug–Sep 2025. Since then it has been flat at roughly 3.3–3.5%, and it was 3.5% in Aug 2026.
- **Compared with prices overall:** Sydney's all-groups CPI was up 3.9% over the year to Aug 2026. Rents at 3.5% are therefore growing slightly slower than general prices. That is a change from 2023–24, when rents were outpacing inflation.
- **Compared with the national figure:** Sydney was well above the national rent figure in 2023–24. It is now level with it, at 3.5% against 3.6%.

**Cumulative effect:** Rent levels haven't fallen. Chaining the annual rates gives my own rough estimate that Sydney rents are about 14% higher than in Aug 2023. The three annual rates behind that are 7.1%, 3.2% and 3.5%. Including the 8.7% rise in the year to Aug 2023, the total is roughly 24% over four years. A slowdown in growth means rents are rising more slowly, not getting cheaper.

**What this doesn't show**
- The CPI rents measure covers rents paid by all tenants, including those on existing leases. It lags what new renters face, and asking rents on new listings can be higher.
- It also doesn't show rent levels, affordability relative to income, or vacancy rates. My ABS search didn't turn up a dataset for those.

Overall, the worst of the acceleration looks to be over. Rents are still rising at about 3.5% a year on top of the large increases already locked in, so affordability remains stretched even though the pace has eased.
